lede: Two identical lumps of chalk, one crushed, dropped into the same acid: one fizzes for a minute, the other for five. Rate is how fast a reaction goes, and this topic is about measuring it and reading it off a graph.
can: Use rate = change divided by time, and rate = 1 divided by time, with the right units.
Choose apparatus for the gas-volume, mass-loss and disappearing-cross methods.
Read a total, a finishing time and a rate off a volume-against-time curve.

text: Measuring the rate of a reaction

md: Two lumps of chalk dropped into the same acid fizz for very different lengths of time if one of them has been crushed. Rate is simply how fast the change happens, and the whole of this topic is about measuring that speed and reading it off a graph.

prompt: In the apparatus shown, which piece of equipment measures the volume of gas?
explain: The gas syringe. Write the word gas as well: 'syringe' on its own was recorded as a lost mark in Summer 2025.

text: 1. Rate is a change divided by a time

md:
A **rate** tells you how much something changes in each second. So you measure **how much** the reaction has done and **how long** it took, and divide:
**rate = change ÷ time**.
The change can be a volume of gas made, in cm³, or a mass lost, in g. The unit of the rate follows straight from that: cm³/s or g/s.

title: Why the flask gets lighter
md: Nothing is destroyed. The carbon dioxide made in the flask escapes through the cotton wool into the room, and the mass it takes with it is the mass the balance stops seeing. That is why the loss in mass measures how much reaction has happened.

prompt: In the balance experiment shown, 3.60 g of gas had escaped after 200 s. Work out the mean rate in g/s, to three decimal places.
explain: 3.60 ÷ 200 = 0.018 g/s. Change first, time second, and the unit is the change's unit over seconds.

text: 2. Three ways to follow the same reaction

md: CCEA limits you to three methods. **Collect the gas** in a gas syringe and read its volume. **Weigh the flask** and watch the mass fall. Or, where a **precipitate** forms, time how long the mixture takes to turn cloudy enough to hide a cross printed underneath. For the cross there is no volume and no mass, so the rate is written **rate = 1 ÷ time**, in s⁻¹.

prompt: In the disappearing-cross experiment shown, the cross could no longer be seen after 32 s. Use rate = 1 ÷ time to find the rate, in s⁻¹, to three decimal places.
explain: 1 ÷ 32 = 0.031 s⁻¹. A longer time means a smaller rate, which is the whole point of writing it upside down.

caption: Steep at the start, flat at the end: the two places questions always ask about.

md: Plot volume against time and the curve tells you three things. Its **steepness** is the rate, so the reaction is fastest at the **start**. Where it **goes flat** the reaction has stopped, because a reactant has run out: here that is at 50 s. And the **height** of that flat stretch is the **total** volume made, 54 cm³ — read it off the plateau, never by adding up the table.

title: Where this mark goes
md: In Summer 2025's Chemistry Booklet B a sizeable number **added every volume in the table together** instead of reading the total off the flat stretch. The syringe reading is already a running total, so the last one is the whole amount.

prompt: On the volume-against-time curve above, the line runs flat from 50 s onwards. What total volume of gas was made, in cm³?
explain: 54 cm³, the height of the flat stretch. Summer 2025's Booklet B report records a sizeable number of candidates adding every volume in the table instead, which gives a far larger nonsense figure.

md:
**The question.** Use the graph to calculate the mean rate of reaction between 20 s and 40 s. Give your answer in cm³/s.
**Step 1 — read both volumes, not one.** At 20 s the syringe holds 36 cm³; at 40 s it holds 52 cm³.
**Step 2 — take the change.** 52 − 36 = 16 cm³. This is the step the dashed lines draw.

prompt: Finish step 2 for the same curve: the volume rises from 36 cm³ at 20 s to 52 cm³ at 40 s. What is the change in volume, in cm³?
explain: 52 − 36 = 16 cm³. Subtracting is the step that most answers skip, and reading 52 straight off the axis is the commonest wrong route.

md:
**Step 3 — divide by the time taken.** The time is 40 − 20 = 20 s, not 40 s.
**Step 4 — divide and keep the unit.** 16 ÷ 20 = 0.8 cm³/s.
Compare it with the very start, where the curve climbs 22 cm³ in the first 10 s: a rate of 2.2 cm³/s. The reaction really has slowed down, because the acid is being used up.

prompt: Use the same rule on the whole reaction: 54 cm³ of gas was collected and the curve went flat at 50 s. Give the mean rate in cm³/s, to two decimal places.
explain: 54 ÷ 50 = 1.08 cm³/s. Divide by the time the reaction actually took, not by the last time printed in the table.

md: Run the same reaction faster and the curve is **steeper and finishes earlier** — but it stops at the **same height**, because the same 2.0 g of calcium carbonate can only ever make the same amount of gas. A sketch that finishes higher or lower than the original is the mark examiners take away most often on this topic.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Mean Rate of Reaction"
why: Watch a mean rate worked straight off a curve, then come back and do the gate.

prompt: The reaction in the graph above is repeated with the same 2.0 g of calcium carbonate but with the chips crushed to a powder. Where does the new curve finish?
options: at the same height, 54 cm³, but sooner
higher than 54 cm³, because it is faster
lower than 54 cm³, because it finishes early
answer: at the same height, 54 cm³, but sooner
explain: The same height. Speed changes when the gas arrives, not how much there is: 54 cm³ either way.

title: Not on this specification
md: Other boards ask for the rate at a single instant by **drawing a tangent** to the curve, and the videos for this topic show it. CCEA does not examine tangents: a mean rate between two times is as far as you are asked to go.

prompt: On a volume-against-time curve, the reaction has stopped where the line goes ______.
explain: Flat. No more gas is arriving, so a reactant has been used up.

md:
use **rate = change ÷ time**, with the unit cm³/s or g/s.
use **rate = 1 ÷ time** for a disappearing cross, in s⁻¹.
name the three methods CCEA allows and the apparatus each one needs.
read the total made from the **plateau** and the finishing time from where the curve goes flat.
sketch a faster run: steeper, earlier, **same finishing height**.

Rates is Question 7 of C2 and Question 2 of Chemistry Booklet B. The first mark is usually a reading taken straight off the curve; the last is the rate to the accuracy the stem names. Stuck? Write **rate = change ÷ time**, then say which change and which time you are using. The Sheet below lists the traps.
